overview.title: Information bottlenecks and further experiments
overview.section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example
overview.main_topic: Equivalence of the sparse loss; the effect of a 4-unit intermediate layer on a 46-class problem; suggested experiments with layer sizes and depth
overview.central_idea: Squeezing the representation through a 4-dimensional layer before a 46-way classifier loses information: validation accuracy peaks around 71%, about 8 points lower than the 64-unit model. Intermediate layers should not be much smaller than the number of output classes.
overview.importance: It turns the abstract warning about information bottlenecks (p.142-143) into a measured experiment, giving a concrete rule of thumb for sizing hidden layers in classifiers.

summary:
The page first finishes section 4.2.6: **`sparse_categorical_crossentropy` is mathematically the same as `categorical_crossentropy`**; it just has a different interface (integer targets instead of one-hot).

**4.2.7 The importance of having sufficiently large intermediate layers.** The authors recall their earlier warning (p.142-143): because the outputs are 46-dimensional, intermediate layers with much fewer than 46 units should be avoided. To show why, **listing 4.23** builds a model with an **information bottleneck**: `Dense(64, relu)` → `Dense(4, relu)` → `Dense(46, softmax)`. It is compiled as before (Adam, categorical crossentropy, accuracy) and trained on `partial_x_train` for 20 epochs with `batch_size=128`, monitoring `(x_val, y_val)`.

Result: validation accuracy now **peaks at about 71%, an 8% absolute drop**. The authors attribute this mostly to trying to compress "enough information to recover the separation hyperplanes of 46 classes" into a space that is too low-dimensional. The model manages to cram *most* (italicized in the book) of the necessary information into the 4-dimensional representations, but not all of it.

**4.2.8 Further experiments.** As with IMDb, the authors suggest experiments to build intuition about configuration choices:

- try larger or smaller layers: 32 units, 128 units, and so on;
- try a single intermediate layer, or three, instead of the two used before the softmax layer.

Note (not in the book): listing 4.23 also changes `batch_size` from 512 to 128, so it is not a perfectly controlled comparison, but the size of the drop and the reasoning about dimensionality make the bottleneck the main cause, as the book says ("mostly due to").

paragraphs.what_it_says: The sparse loss computes the same thing as categorical crossentropy; only the interface differs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Given an integer label c, sparse crossentropy returns $-\log \hat y_c$; given the one-hot version of c, categorical crossentropy returns $-\sum_i y_i\log\hat y_i$, which is the same number. Gradients, and therefore training, are identical.

paragraphs.what_it_means: In a stack of Dense layers each layer sees only the previous layer's output (p.142). If a layer has 4 units, everything the classifier knows about a newswire must pass through 4 numbers, which may be too few to keep 46 topics apart.

concepts.name: Information bottleneck
concepts.definition: A layer whose dimensionality is too low to carry all the information later layers need, permanently discarding some of it.
concepts.intuition: Describing a 46-way topic choice with only 4 numbers is like summarizing an article in 4 words: much survives, not everything.
concepts.technical: Listing 4.23 inserts `Dense(4, relu)` between `Dense(64)` and `Dense(46, softmax)`; validation accuracy peaks near 71% instead of about 79-80%.
concepts.significance: Gives a rule of thumb: intermediate layers should not be much narrower than the number of classes.
concepts.example: 64 → 4 → 46 units: 260 weights in the 4-unit layer must encode everything the 46-way classifier sees.
concepts.misconception: That smaller layers are always better for generalization because they have fewer parameters; too small a layer underfits by destroying information.

concepts.name: Sparse categorical crossentropy
concepts.definition: Crossentropy loss that takes integer labels.
concepts.intuition: Same loss, label given as an index.
concepts.technical: Equal to categorical crossentropy on one-hot labels.
concepts.misconception: That it trains differently; it is mathematically the same.

concepts.name: Dense layer width
concepts.definition: The number of units in a Dense layer, i.e., the dimensionality of its output representation.
concepts.intuition: How many numbers each sample is described by at that stage.
concepts.technical: A Dense(n) layer on m inputs has $m\cdot n + n$ parameters; widths here are 64, 4 and 46.
concepts.significance: Width controls both capacity and the information that can flow onward.
concepts.misconception: Width only affects parameter count; it also caps the rank of the information passed on.

math.title: Why a 4-unit layer limits the 46 logits
math.latex: z = W_3\,h + b_3, \quad h = \operatorname{relu}(W_2 a + b_2) \in \mathbb{R}^4,\; W_3 \in \mathbb{R}^{46\times 4} \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{rank}(W_3) \le 4
math.source_text: layers.Dense(4, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(46, activation="softmax") (the formula is not printed in the book)

variables.meaning: 64-dimensional output of the first Dense layer
Weights (46×4) and bias (46) of the softmax layer

math.operations: The final layer maps 4 numbers to 46 logits linearly; its image is at most a 4-dimensional affine subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{46}$.
math.purpose: Makes precise the book's statement that the intermediate space is "too low-dimensional".
math.interpretation: Any information about the input that does not survive in $h$ cannot affect the prediction, and the space of achievable logit patterns is restricted.
math.intuition: 46 class scores are being driven by only 4 knobs.
math.numerical_example: With 64 hidden units the logits can span up to 46 dimensions (since $64 \ge 46$); with 4 units, at most 4 (plus the fixed bias offset).

math.title: Parameter counts of the bottleneck model
math.source_text: Dense(64) → Dense(4) → Dense(46) on 10,000-dimensional multi-hot inputs

variables.meaning: Units in the three Dense layers

math.operations: Weights (inputs × units) plus biases (units) per layer.
math.purpose: Shows that the bottleneck barely changes the total parameter count (vs. 647,214 for 64-64-46), so the accuracy drop is about representation width, not overall capacity.
math.interpretation: Removing about 6,700 parameters from a 647k-parameter model costs 8 accuracy points because of where they are removed.
math.intuition: The narrowest pipe, not the total volume, limits the flow.

code.title: A model with an information bottleneck
code.original_code:
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(4, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(46, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    partial_x_train,
    partial_y_train,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=128,
    validation_data=(x_val, y_val),
)
code.what_it_does: Trains a 64-4-46 model on the 7,982-sample training split for 20 epochs, monitoring validation accuracy, to show the effect of a too-narrow hidden layer.

deeper.title: Bottleneck: too little width vs. too many parameters
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the 64-64-46 and 64-4-46 models have nearly the same number of parameters (647k vs. 641k), since almost all are in the first layer. The difference is that the second model forces every newswire through a 4-number summary. This illustrates that a network's *shape* matters, not just its size: the narrowest layer caps the information available downstream.

deeper.title: Running the suggested experiments well
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): 1. Keep everything fixed except one setting (width or depth). 2. Train with the same validation split and record the best `val_accuracy` and the epoch it occurs. 3. Compare against the 64-64-46 reference (≈82% peak validation, p.145). 4. Expect diminishing returns for widths above 64 and earlier overfitting for wider or deeper models.

misconceptions.claim: Making a hidden layer very small is a good way to prevent overfitting.
misconceptions.correction: It may reduce overfitting, but if the layer is too narrow it destroys information needed for the task, as the 71% result shows.

misconceptions.claim: The 8% drop means accuracy fell by 8% of its value.
misconceptions.correction: The book says "absolute": about 8 percentage points.

misconceptions.claim: Later layers can recover information dropped by an earlier narrow layer.
misconceptions.correction: Each Dense layer only sees the previous layer's output, so dropped information is lost permanently (p.142-143).

takeaways: `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and `categorical_crossentropy` are mathematically the same; only the label format differs.
Hidden layers much narrower than the number of classes create information bottlenecks.
A 4-unit hidden layer drops peak validation accuracy to about 71%, an 8-point absolute loss.
The model can fit most, but not all, of the needed information into 4 dimensions.

questions.question: What is the only architectural difference between listing 4.23 and listing 4.15?
options: The second hidden layer has 4 units instead of 64
The first hidden layer uses softmax
There is an extra hidden layer
questions.answer: The second hidden layer has 4 units instead of 64
questions.explanation: The output is still Dense(46, softmax), the first layer is still Dense(64, relu), and there are still two hidden layers.

questions.question: What validation accuracy does the bottleneck model reach, and how does the book explain the drop?
questions.answer: About 71%, an 8% absolute drop, mostly because information needed to separate 46 classes is compressed into a 4-dimensional space that is too small.
questions.explanation: The book says the model crams most, but not all, of the necessary information into the 4-dimensional representations.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does the Dense(4) layer have, and how many does the Dense(46) layer after it have?
questions.explanation: Each Dense layer has inputs × units weights plus one bias per unit.

questions.question: The bottleneck model has almost the same total number of parameters as the 64-64-46 model. Why does it perform much worse?
questions.answer: Because nearly all parameters are in the first layer; what matters is that every sample's representation must pass through 4 numbers, which cannot carry all the information needed to separate 46 topics.
questions.explanation: The book attributes the drop to the low dimensionality of the intermediate space; the parameter comparison is an AI-added illustration.

questions.question: Why can `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` replace `categorical_crossentropy` without changing training results?
options: It uses a different but approximately equal formula
It is mathematically the same loss; it only takes integer labels instead of one-hot
It only works for binary problems
questions.answer: It is mathematically the same loss; it only takes integer labels instead of one-hot
questions.explanation: The book states it is mathematically the same with a different interface. It is not an approximation, it uses the softmax output, and it works for any number of classes.

questions.question: Besides the hidden-layer width, what else differs between the training call in listing 4.23 and listing 4.18, and why does that matter for interpreting the result?
questions.answer: The batch size is 128 instead of 512. Strictly, two variables changed, so a fully controlled comparison would keep the batch size at 512; the large drop and the dimensionality argument still point to the bottleneck as the main cause.
questions.explanation: This is an observation about the code, not a point the book makes; the book says the drop is "mostly" due to the bottleneck.

questions.question: Plan the two experiments of section 4.2.8: which settings would you vary, what would you hold fixed, and what result would you record?
questions.answer: Vary hidden width (e.g., 32, 64, 128) with two layers, then vary depth (1, 2, 3 layers) at 64 units; keep data split, optimizer, loss, epochs and batch size fixed; record peak validation accuracy and the epoch at which it occurs.
questions.explanation: This follows the book's suggestions and the one-variable-at-a-time principle.
